title: ISC2 CISSP-ISSMP
summary: The Information Systems Security Management Professional (ISSMP) is an advanced concentration exam from ISC2 for people who already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) and want to be judged on management rather than hands on engineering. It suits security managers, programme leads and consultants who own budgets, policy and staff. It proves to an employer that you can build a security programme, lead a team, argue for funding and keep the organisation running through a serious incident. The exam is multiple choice and tests judgement at the level of a manager, so the questions read like the decisions you make in a weekly leadership meeting rather than like configuration tasks. It leads to roles such as security manager, security programme director, governance lead and chief information security officer. The domain structure below follows the published objectives; ISC2 has refreshed this outline, so check the vendor's current version and weighting before you book. This is an independent study guide and is not official ISC2 material.

beginner.definition: The Information Systems Security Management Professional (ISSMP) is an advanced certificate from ISC2. It is open only to people who already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP). It tests whether you can manage a programme, a budget and a team. It does not test whether you can configure a firewall.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security careers slow down when the work stops being technical. This certificate shows an employer that you can run a whole programme. It is a strong signal for manager, director and governance roles. It also builds on the leadership side of the CISSP. The core exam only touches that side lightly. That makes it useful for a job where you own policy and people.
howItWorks: Check that you already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP). This exam is only open to holders.
Read the official ISC2 exam outline and list every domain. Then write down the tasks under each one.
Study security governance, risk management, and contingency planning, which carry the largest share of questions.
Learn how to build a business case and set a budget. Then learn to report risk to senior leaders.
Practise scenario questions where several answers are defensible and you must pick the best management choice.
The exam is multiple choice, so plan several months of study around your current job.
beginner.example: Picture a ransomware attack at a hospital. A team lead asks which backup to restore first. A security manager asks different questions. Who decides whether to pay? Who talks to patients and regulators? How long can each service stay down? Who signs off when the recovery plan changes? The ISSMP exam lives in that second set of questions. It rewards people who can hold a plan together while everyone else is under pressure.
takeaways: You must already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) before you sit this exam.
The questions test management judgement, so study decision making and not only definitions.
Expect to justify spending, staffing and risk decisions to a senior audience.

objectives: Build a security programme that matches the organisation's strategy and risk appetite
Lead and organise a security team, including hiring, training and measuring performance
Run enterprise risk management and explain the results to senior leaders
Use threat modelling to shape which controls the organisation funds first
Write and test contingency plans that keep critical services running during an incident

chapters.title: Security leadership and management
objectives: Set a security strategy that supports the business plan and the organisation's risk appetite
Design an organisational structure for security and define who is accountable for what
Build a security budget and justify each item in business terms
Recruit, develop and retain security staff, including succession for key roles
Define security roles, responsibilities and ethics for the whole workforce

chapters.title: Systems development and lifecycle management
objectives: Build security requirements into each stage of a system's life, from concept to retirement
Choose development and acquisition methods that keep security work visible
Set change control so that updates are tested, approved and recorded
Plan how data and hardware are securely removed when a system is retired
Review supplier and third party software before it enters the environment

chapters.title: Risk management
objectives: Define a risk management process that covers identification, analysis, treatment and monitoring
Choose between qualitative and quantitative methods and explain the trade offs
Set risk tolerance and escalation rules that managers can apply without asking you
Report risk in a form that executives and auditors can act on
Track treatment plans to completion and confirm that the risk really dropped

chapters.title: Threat modeling
objectives: Identify the threats and attack patterns that matter most to your organisation
Model threats against a system and map them to the controls that reduce them
Use threat intelligence to update the model as the attacker picture changes
Prioritise findings so that limited budget goes to the highest real risk
Brief technical teams and executives on the same threat picture without losing either audience

chapters.title: Contingency planning
objectives: Run a business impact analysis that sets recovery priorities and time targets
Write business continuity and disaster recovery plans that staff can follow under stress
Design backup, alternate site and continuity arrangements for critical services
Test plans through exercises, then correct the gaps the tests reveal
Keep plans alive as systems, suppliers and people change
